name: Preparation H under eyes
lead: Preparation H under eyes is an off-label beauty practice in which the hemorrhoid product Preparation H is dabbed on the skin beneath the eyes to reduce puffiness and bags, so the area looks smoother, tighter and more rested. It circulates in beauty lore as a quick pharmacy-counter de-puffing trick, usually reached for before a photo, event or early morning, and is often attributed to models and makeup artists, though published sources do not document its origin.

Preparation H is an American brand made by Pfizer, sold as water-based gels, petroleum-jelly ointments, cocoa-butter suppositories and medicated wipes. Active ingredients vary by version and country and include phenylephrine (0.25 percent in some), hydrocortisone, pramoxine, witch hazel and caffeine, and some versions contain shark liver oil or a yeast extract.[1] Proponents point to phenylephrine, a selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that narrows arteries and veins, as the ingredient that tightens the under-eye area by shrinking visible swelling in the same way it is intended to shrink swollen tissue in hemorrhoids.[2]

No published study has tested the product on periorbital skin, and its labelled use is anorectal. Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles notes that thin lower-lid skin lets underlying vessels show, and that rebound after vasoconstrictors wear off can darken the area.[3] Users therefore tend to describe it as a short-term cosmetic measure, in the same family as cold compresses and caffeine eye products.[6]

chain: Thin gel is dabbed under the eye
A vasoconstrictor ingredient narrows small vessels
The area looks temporarily tighter and less swollen
angle.text: Users apply a small amount under the eyes hoping for a short-lived tightening that reduces bags before an event or photo. The effect is attributed to phenylephrine constricting vessels in thin eyelid skin.

infobox: Phenylephrine 0.25%, hydrocortisone 1%, pramoxine, witch hazel, caffeine; some versions shark liver oil or yeast extract[1]

paras: The original formulation was invented by George Sperti, with a yeast extract as the main ingredient. American Home Products, incorporated in 1926, acquired a sunburn oil in 1935 that became Preparation H, one of the world's best-selling hemorrhoid treatments. The company was renamed Wyeth in 2002, and Pfizer bought Wyeth in 2009.[1]

Sperti (1900 to 1991) was a University of Cincinnati research laboratory director who held 127 patents, including an ultraviolet lamp for adding vitamin D to milk and a method for freeze-drying orange juice concentrate.[5] He named the main active ingredient of his product Bio-Dyne, a live yeast cell derivative whose cell-growth-promoting activity was discovered at the university by Stanley L. Baker. It was first tested on burn victims, and an accidental application led to the large hemorrhoid market. According to Wikipedia, the FDA later found irregularities in the clinical testing of the derivative, and it was removed from the US formulation, while Canadian and European versions still contain it.[5]

Formulations differ by country. The yeast extract, called Biodyne in Canada, was removed from the US formulation in 1995 but remains in the Canadian version, where Pfizer says it removes wrinkles and heals dry, cracked and irritated skin. The Greek version contains 1 percent yeast extract and 3 percent shark liver oil.[1] Wikipedia describes most versions as working by reducing inflammation of blood vessels.[1]

The range runs from simple caffeine moisturizers with witch hazel astringent to products with phenylephrine, pramoxine and hydrocortisone. One version has 1 percent hydrocortisone as its sole active ingredient; others have 0.25 percent phenylephrine together with shark liver oil.[1] Because the ingredients differ so much between gels, ointments and wipes, descriptions of the under-eye trick in popular sources do not always refer to the same product. Wikipedia's hemorrhoid article describes typical hemorrhoid products as combining a barrier cream, an analgesic and a vasoconstrictor, and says steroid-containing products should not be used for more than 14 days because they may thin the skin.[7]

Believers say a thin layer of a phenylephrine-containing gel constricts the small vessels beneath thin eyelid skin and reduces visible swelling and bags within minutes. The idea sits among other quick de-puffing practices such as cold compresses and caffeine eye products. Wikipedia names caffeine as the one vasoconstrictor that eye creams use to tighten dilated vessels under the eyes.[3] Those who describe using the product treat it as a short-term cosmetic fix, not a lasting treatment.

Puffiness and dark circles have several causes. Wikipedia describes eye bags as almost always involving fluid build-up, often worse on waking, with aging, allergy, sleep deprivation, salt intake and other factors contributing; it lists cold compresses as a short-term remedy because cold constricts blood vessels, and head elevation during sleep as a preventive measure.[6] It also lists pigmentation from extra melanin, vascular causes including thin skin that lets blood show through, structural shadows from bone shape and fat descent with age, and a link between dark circles and minor sleep deprivation.[3] A vasoconstrictor addresses only the vascular component. Wikipedia also notes that severe or persistent swelling can signal a condition needing medical evaluation.[6]

In its medical uses phenylephrine narrows blood vessels, which is why it appears in hemorrhoid products and in eye drops that dilate the pupil.[2] Whether the product has a visible effect on the periorbital area has not been tested. Dermatology references describe rebound vasodilation after vasoconstrictors as a possible contributor to darkened skin.[3] A 1984 study examined the product's effect on wound healing in the human rectum, which does not address appearance.[4]

The product is labelled for anorectal use. Hydrocortisone versions are corticosteroids, and eyelid skin is thin.[7] Phenylephrine's documented adverse effects relate to systemic exposure and include raised blood pressure and heart rhythm effects, and it is avoided in people with hypertension, heart disease or narrow-angle glaucoma.[2] No data describe these risks for under-eye application, and getting product in the eye is a concern for any non-ophthalmic preparation.
No studies found for use under the eyes. A 1984 study examined the product's effect on wound healing in the human rectum, which does not address appearance.[4]

lore.intro: The under-eye use is a long-circulating beauty hack, often attributed to models and makeup artists, though published sources do not document its origin.

claims.claim: Preparation H shrinks eye bags by constricting blood vessels.
claims.believers: Users say a dab of the gel tightens the under-eye area for a few hours, citing phenylephrine's vasoconstrictor action.
claims.experts: Phenylephrine does constrict vessels in its labelled uses [2], but no study has tested the product on periorbital skin.

claims.claim: The yeast extract in some versions smooths wrinkles.
claims.believers: Pfizer states that the yeast extract in the Canadian formulation removes wrinkles and heals dry skin [1].
claims.experts: No published trial tests this for wrinkles; the extract was removed from the US formulation in 1995 [1].

claims.claim: Vasoconstrictors can darken the area afterward.
claims.believers: Some users warn that circles look worse when the effect wears off.
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists rebound after vasoconstrictors wear off as one vascular cause of darker periorbital skin [3].

claims.claim: Cold compresses, caffeine and Preparation H all work the same way
claims.believers: Beauty writers and users group the product with other vasoconstricting de-puffers such as cold compresses and caffeine creams.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes cold as constricting vessels and caffeine as the vasoconstrictor used in eye creams; only the product's phenylephrine and caffeine versions are mechanistically similar, and none of its versions have been tested under the eyes.[3][6]

card.summary: Hemorrhoid cream dabbed under the eyes on the theory that its vasoconstrictor shrinks bags; no studies support or test the practice.
card.note: Off-label; some formulations contain hydrocortisone and the product is not made for eyelids.

quick.overview:
Some people apply Preparation H, a hemorrhoid treatment, to the skin under the eyes, reasoning that its blood-vessel constrictor will reduce puffiness. The idea circulates as a beauty hack.
No clinical study of this use was found, and the product is labelled for hemorrhoids.
quick.mechanism: Some versions contain 0.25% phenylephrine, a vasoconstrictor, and shark liver oil; others use 1% hydrocortisone or other actives. Proponents say vasoconstriction shrinks swelling. Formulations differ by country.
quick.risks: The product is made for anorectal use, not eyelids. Dermatology references note that vasoconstrictors can be followed by rebound darkening, and steroid versions raise skin-thinning concerns. No safety data for periorbital use were found.
